title: X86ASM 10: Write Your Own Print Function

questions.q: Before executing `syscall`, which register tells the kernel which kernel function you want (for example, write vs. exit)?
choices: RDI
RSI
RAX
RDX
questions.explain: The syscall number goes in RAX, and it is set before `syscall` runs, because arguments are always filled in before a function executes.

questions.q: What value is moved into RAX to request the write system call on Linux x86-64?
questions.explain: RAX = 1 selects write.

questions.q: For the write syscall, which register holds the number of bytes to print?
choices: RCX
RDX
RSI
RAX
questions.explain: write takes the file descriptor in RDI, the buffer address in RSI, and the length in RDX.

questions.q: In the print function's write call, which statements are correct?
choices: RDI is set to 1 to write to standard output (the terminal)
RSI holds the address of the first byte of the string
RDX holds the length of the string
RCX holds the file descriptor
RSI holds the full contents of the string
questions.explain: RDI = 1 (stdout), RSI = start address, RDX = length. A register holds only the address of the string, not the whole string.

questions.q: Why does write need both a starting address and a length instead of just "the string"?
choices: Because write can only print one character per call
Because the kernel always prints exactly 64 bytes unless told otherwise
Because strings in the data segment are stored in reverse order
Because no addressing mode can refer to the whole string; you only have the address of its first byte, so the length says how many bytes to read from there
questions.explain: A label like s1 marks only the first byte. The kernel starts reading there and uses the length to know when to stop.

questions.q: What does `lea rsi, [s1]` do?
choices: Loads the address of label s1 (the string's first byte) into RSI
Loads the first 8 bytes of the string into RSI
Copies the whole string into the RSI register
Stores the value of RSI into memory at s1
questions.explain: LEA (load effective address) puts the computed address itself into the register. It does not read the memory there.

questions.q: To pass print's string argument on to write, both `mov rsi, rdi` and `lea rsi, [rdi]` work: each puts the string's address into RSI.
questions.explain: mov copies the register value. lea with [rdi] computes the address RDI + 0, which is the same value.

questions.q: Which list gives the six System V integer argument registers in the correct order?
choices: RAX, RBX, RCX, RDX, RSI, RDI
RSI, RDI, RDX, RCX, R8, R9
RDI, RSI, RDX, RCX, R8, R9
RDI, RSI, RCX, RDX, R8, R9
questions.explain: The order is RDI, RSI, RDX, RCX, R8, R9. That is why write's arguments land in RDI, RSI, RDX.

questions.q: Under the System V convention, where does a function's 7th integer argument go?
choices: On the stack
RAX
It cannot be passed; functions are limited to six arguments
questions.explain: Six registers carry arguments. Any further arguments go on the stack.

questions.q: By convention, which register holds a function's return value (for example, the length returned by strlen)?
questions.explain: Return values go in RAX.

questions.q: Inside print, why must `mov rdx, rax` come right after `call _strlen` and before `mov rax, 1`?
choices: Because RDX must be set before RDI, or the kernel rejects the call
Because strlen returns its result in RDX and it has to be copied into RAX
Because `mov rax, 1` automatically clears RDX
Because strlen returns the length in RAX, and loading the syscall number into RAX would overwrite that length
questions.explain: The length is in RAX after the call. Copy it into RDX, where write expects it, before RAX is reused for the syscall number.

questions.q: Because print and strlen both take their first argument in RDI, print does not have to move anything into RDI before calling strlen with the string it received.
questions.explain: The caller already put the string address in RDI for print, and that is exactly where strlen expects it. Writing `mov rdi, rdi` would be redundant.

questions.q: What is the name of the calling convention (application binary interface) used on Linux that fixes the argument order RDI, RSI, RDX, ...?
questions.explain: The System V ABI standardizes register use so code from different authors agrees on where arguments and return values go.

questions.q: Declaring a string with `.asciz` adds a terminating zero byte, which strlen uses to find the end of the string.
questions.explain: strlen loops over the bytes until it reaches the null terminator (0).

questions.q: After strlen finishes, the debugger shows 0xD in RAX. What string length is that in decimal?
The `\n` escape at the end of a string adds two characters to its length: a backslash and an n.
questions.explain: `\n` is a single newline character and counts as one byte.

questions.q: With the original strlen, printing one string worked, but printing a second string afterward printed too many characters. What caused this?
choices: RCX, the counter, was never reset, so each call added onto the previous length
RAX was never incremented, so the loop never advanced
The second string was missing its newline
write always prints every string in the data segment
questions.explain: strlen counted in RCX but never cleared it. The second call started from the first string's length and returned a total that was too large.

questions.q: To fix the strlen bug, where should `xor rcx, rcx` go?
choices: Right after `inc rcx` inside the loop
At the top of the loop, before `mov bl, [rax]`
In strlen's setup code, before the loop label
After `ret`
questions.explain: Clear the counter once when strlen starts. If you clear it inside the loop, it gets reset on every pass and every string comes out with length 0. Anything after `ret` never runs.

questions.q: What advantage does calling strlen at runtime have over computing a string's length at assembly time (as in a basic hello-world program)?
choices: It makes the program use less memory
It works for any string, including ones whose length isn't known when the program is assembled
It lets you skip the null terminator
It lets write run without a length argument
questions.explain: A length computed at assembly time only works for fixed strings. Counting at runtime makes print work for any string.

questions.q: print passes its string to strlen in RDI and still needs that value after strlen returns. Who is responsible for making sure RDI still holds it?
choices: strlen (the callee) must restore RDI before returning
print (the caller) must save RDI itself, for example on the stack
The kernel saves RDI automatically on every call
No one; `call` preserves all registers
questions.explain: RDI is caller-saved. strlen makes no promise to keep it unchanged, so print has to save it if it cares about the value.

questions.q: In this lesson strlen never modifies RDI, so copying RDI into RSI after the call without saving it first is good practice and will always be safe.
questions.explain: It only happens to work. strlen, or some function it calls later, could clobber RDI, so print should save and restore it.

questions.q: Which instruction order in print correctly protects RDI across the strlen call and then sets up write's length and buffer?
choices: call _strlen / push rdi / pop rdi / mov rdx, rax / mov rsi, rdi
push rdi / pop rdi / call _strlen / mov rdx, rax / mov rsi, rdi
pop rdi / call _strlen / push rdi / mov rdx, rax / mov rsi, rdi
push rdi / call _strlen / pop rdi / mov rdx, rax / mov rsi, rdi
questions.explain: Push before the call so the value is safe, then pop after the call returns to restore it. Only then copy the length and the string address.

questions.q: To demonstrate the problem, strlen was changed to zero RDI, and print did not save it. What happened when the program ran?
choices: The program crashed with a segmentation fault
The string was printed twice
Nothing was printed, and the program still exited with code 0
Random bytes from address 0 were printed
questions.explain: RSI received 0 as the buffer address. The kernel found nothing to print there, so no output appeared, but the program still exited normally with code 0.

questions.q: print runs `push rdi`, then `call _strlen` (which zeroes RDI), then `pop rdi`. What is true after the pop?
choices: RDI holds the original string address again, and that saved value has been removed from the stack
RDI is 0, because pop cannot undo changes made inside another function
RDI holds strlen's return address
RDI holds the string length
questions.explain: pop copies the top of the stack (the saved address) into RDI and removes it from the stack, so print continues as if strlen never touched RDI.

questions.q: What value goes in RAX to ask the kernel to end the process (the exit syscall)?
questions.explain: RAX = 60 selects exit. RDI holds the exit code.

questions.q: Which instructions set RDI to 0 (for example, to exit with status 0)?
choices: xor rdi, rdi
inc rdi
mov rdi, 0
push rdi
questions.explain: Both xor rdi, rdi and mov rdi, 0 zero the register. The lesson prefers xor because it is slightly more efficient.

questions.q: What does the `call` instruction do?
choices: Jumps to the target and saves the return address in RCX
Runs a kernel function selected by RAX
Pushes the return address (the address of the next instruction) onto the stack, then jumps to the target
Pops an address off the stack and jumps to it
questions.explain: call pushes the return address and then jumps. Later, ret pops that address so execution resumes on the line after the call.

questions.q: When `call` pushes a return address such as 0x401005, the address bytes are stored on the stack in little-endian order.
questions.explain: x86-64 is little-endian, so the least significant byte is stored at the lowest address.

questions.q: After print's syscall, the program crashed because execution ran straight into strlen's code. What fixes this?
choices: Moving the data section above the code
Placing the exit syscall (mov rax, 60 / xor rdi, rdi / syscall) at the end of the main code, before the function definitions
Adding an extra `ret` at the very start of strlen
Clearing RCX at the top of print
questions.explain: Without an exit, the CPU just keeps executing whatever bytes come next. Ending the main code with exit, and putting functions below it, keeps execution from falling into them.

questions.q: What is `int3` (interrupt 3) used for while testing the print function?
choices: Calling the write syscall
Returning from a function
Clearing a register
Acting as a breakpoint, so a debugger can stop and you can inspect registers after continuing
questions.explain: int3 traps to the debugger, so you can press continue and stop at that spot (for example, just before strlen returns) without stepping through every loop iteration.
